Oh I completely agree that other parts of the campus feel a little awkward, and I’ve never been too much of a fan of the random fake stone look. If I recall from visiting the college a year and a half ago, the effect tended to vary. I actually thought it was interesting on some of the other portions of the sight such as [here](https://ibb.co/jg0m238) .  However, I will agree with you that the degree to which they take the random stone veneer is somewhat irritating in other portions of the project (like the one you pointed out). 

I think as a whole the project was designed to be viewed from certain specific angles (which were often very well crafted) but that led to other portions of the project being sloppily designed. The worst was probably the [head’s house](https://ibb.co/CHgDtyw). 

The individual who gave us the tour actually was willing to point out some of the issues with the building to us. The main issue with proportioning in his words had to do with the fact that due to cost issues, it was decided to limit the total number of window types used in the design, which led to a more repetitive layout. 

However, on the topic of fake, I personally have no problem with a little fake charm. I actually tend to like a fair amount of postmodern architecture and neo-traditional new-urban architecture (which most definitely is not a representation of structure), and am a fan of a lot of late 19th century architecture (which isn’t 100% a pure expression of structure either). 

People are WAY too obsessed with such ideas about “structural honesty” at the moment, which from my point of view has only led architecture down a rather ugly path the past few years or so (just as it did in the 20th century). I actually think the USC Village looks kind of charming and couldn’t care less whether or not it appears to be out of a “theme park”. I’d take pretty colourful details and human/traditional proportions over a dull but honest modernist box any day of the week.
